passage:
I'm Tanvir. In my second year of college, I spent eight months on a study-planner app that nobody used. Twelve downloads, and six were my friends.

Meanwhile, I'd made a small quiz website for my hostel as a joke. Three hundred people used it in a week. Afreen said, "Build that out!" I didn't. I shut it down after a month. I told myself I'd had my fun with it.

But the planner app? I kept adding features. Every time I thought of stopping, I felt a sting in my chest. Eight months, gone. So I kept going, month after month, hoping the numbers would turn.

Looking back, I let go of the winner too early because I was afraid of losing what it had given me. And I held the loser because stopping meant feeling the loss.

This year I restarted the quiz site. It's doing fine.

qa.q: How many downloads did Tanvir's study-planner app get?
qa.a: Twelve downloads, and six were my friends.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir keep working on the planner app?
qa.a: Tanvir felt a sting at the thought of eight months being gone, so continuing felt easier than accepting the loss.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do differently with the next project?
qa.a: Tanvir could set a clear check-in date and ask honestly whether to keep going, and grow the ideas that are working instead of ending them early.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Tanvir shut down the quiz site?
qa.a: Afreen may have felt disappointed and puzzled, since Afreen saw the quiz site's success and encouraged building it out.

Mentor's note, college enterprise club

Jeevan's team ran a food stall at the fest this week. On day one, their lemonade sold out by noon; their momos barely sold at all.

On day two, Jeevan decided to stop making lemonade. "We've made enough on it," he said. He doubled the momos. When I asked why, he said, "We've spent so much on the steamer. If we stop the momos, all that is lost."

By evening they had forty plates of cold momos left.

I sat with the team afterwards. Jeevan looked miserable. I asked, "If you were starting today, which would you sell?" Nandini, his teammate, said "lemonade" before he could answer. He laughed a little.

We talked about how it's painful to admit a loss, so people hold on, and how people cash in on a win early to protect it.

They'll try again next month, lemonade first.

qa.a: Forty plates of cold momos.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan keep making momos on day two?
qa.a: Jeevan felt that stopping would mean the money spent on the steamer was lost, and admitting that loss felt painful.

qa.q: What question did the mentor ask, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: The mentor asked which item they would sell if starting today, which helped the team look forward instead of protecting past spending.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt about Jeevan's choices during the fest?

Dear Nirmala,

You asked how the shift-timing talks went. I noticed something I want to share.

When management first proposed moving our start time from 9 to 8, with the finish moving to 5, the whole floor fought it. People said they were "losing an hour of the morning". Nobody mentioned gaining an hour in the evening, even though it was exactly the same hour.

So I rewrote the proposal. I started with what stays protected: same pay, same lunch break, and evenings free by five for family and classes. Then I was honest: yes, mornings start earlier, and that will be hard for people with school drop-offs. I suggested a flexible option for them.

The mood changed. Not everyone agreed, but the conversation stopped being about losing.

I'm not trying to trick anyone. I just want people to see the whole picture, gains and losses equally.

Lokesh

qa.a: Moving our start time from 9 to 8.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do in rewriting the proposal, and why was it fair?
qa.a: Lokesh led with what stays protected and was honest about what's given up, offering flexibility, so people saw gains and losses together.

qa.a: Those staff may still feel worried about mornings, but feel heard because the proposal admits the difficulty and offers a flexible option.

You asked what I learned from the office move, Deepak. I'm Amandeep, I work in operations, and I watched something fascinating.

When the company said we'd move to a new building with bigger desks but no dedicated parking, people were furious. "We're losing our parking!" Nobody talked about the bigger desks, the better canteen, the metro station next door.

Then someone proposed the reverse: keep parking, but no bigger desks. Hardly anyone cared. They weren't fighting to gain desks. They were fighting not to lose parking.

So when I helped draft the final plan, I wrote it differently. First: what you keep. Same team, same hours, same salary. Then: what you gain. Then, honestly: what you lose, and what we're doing about it. We arranged shared parking with a nearby mall.

People still grumbled. But they stopped feeling robbed. I think honesty about the loss mattered as much as showing the gains.

qa.a: We arranged shared parking with a nearby mall.

qa.a: Amandeep felt fascinated and curious, noticing people fought much harder to keep parking than to gain bigger desks.

qa.q: How did Amandeep's drafting approach help?
qa.a: Amandeep listed what people keep, what they gain and, honestly, what they lose with a fix, so people felt informed rather than robbed.

qa.q: How might the staff who drove to work see the final plan?
qa.a: Drivers might still feel annoyed about losing dedicated parking, but relieved that the shared parking was arranged.

I sat in on the contract renewal with our biggest client. I'm Anand, a junior analyst. My colleague Amandeep led it. Here's what I saw.

The client wanted to cut our monthly reporting and add a quarterly strategy meeting. Our team lead was about to say no. "We'll lose the monthly reports!"

Amandeep asked for a break. In the corridor he said, "Watch how everyone's fighting to keep the reports. Nobody's even thinking about what the strategy meeting gives us."

Back in the room, he said, "Here's what we protect: the client relationship, the same fee, and the key data. Here's what we give up: the monthly reports. Here's what we gain: direct time with their leadership."

He didn't hide the loss. He just put it next to the gain.

The team lead nodded slowly. The renewal went through. I don't know what Amandeep felt exactly, but he looked calm the whole time.

qa.a: A quarterly strategy meeting.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling while watching Amandeep in the meeting?
qa.a: Anand seemed impressed and a little surprised, noticing how calm Amandeep stayed while others fought to keep the reports.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep's framing work in the meeting?
qa.a: Amandeep listed what was protected, what was given up and what was gained, so the loss was honest but no longer the only thing people saw.

qa.q: How might the team lead have felt after Amandeep's framing?
qa.a: The team lead may have felt reassured and less defensive, seeing the renewal as a trade rather than a pure loss.

passage:
Tuesday night

The Pune offer came through today. Better role, same pay. I should be thrilled. Instead I feel sick.

I spent all evening listing what I'd lose: my flat, my Thursday dance class, being near Bidisha, knowing the city. The list got longer and longer.

Then I noticed I hadn't written a single thing I'd gain.

So I did an experiment. I imagined losing the dance class. How bad? Honestly, a 6. Then I imagined gaining a role where I'd lead a small team, which I've wanted for two years. How good? An 8.

I did it for each thing. Loss of the flat: 5. Gain of new people, new projects: 7.

When I put them side by side, Pune looked better. But my gut still wanted to stay. Losses just shout louder.

I'm going to sleep on it. But I feel calmer. I'm weighing things now, not just panicking.

Rashmi

qa.q: What did Rashmi score losing the dance class?
qa.a: Honestly, a 6.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel before doing the experiment?
qa.a: Rashmi felt sick and anxious, focused only on the growing list of losses.

qa.q: What did Rashmi's experiment do well?
qa.a: Scoring each loss and gain of similar size side by side eased the automatic pull toward staying, so Rashmi could weigh the choice fairly.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel if Rashmi moves to Pune?
qa.a: Bidisha might feel sad to lose having Rashmi nearby, but also happy for Rashmi's new role.

grounding: A thoughtful young adult imagines equal losses and gains for a job move and asks which is truly preferred, easing the tilt to safety.

passage:
In Neelam's village near Nashik, her family had grown onions on the same five acres for thirty years. At twenty-five, Neelam wanted to try grapes on one acre, like the neighbours had.

Her brother Lalit shook his head. "What if we lose the onion money from that acre?"

Neelam felt that fear too. It sat heavy in her stomach. But she did something her agriculture teacher had taught her. She sat on the verandah with a notebook and imagined both sides the same size.

If the grapes failed, they'd lose one acre's onion income for a year. If the grapes worked, they'd gain perhaps twice that, every year after.

"Lalit, imagine losing one acre's onions. Now imagine gaining double that. Which would you really choose, if both felt the same size?"

Lalit was quiet. "The gain. But the loss feels bigger."

"That's the tilt," she said. "Let's ask the agriculture officer about it next week, then decide."

qa.q: How many acres did Neelam's family farm?
qa.a: The same five acres for thirty years.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about trying grapes?
qa.a: Neelam felt the fear of losing the onion money heavy in her stomach, but also hopeful about the gain.

qa.q: What did Neelam do to weigh the choice fairly, and what is her next step?
qa.a: Neelam imagined the loss and gain at the same size to counter the tilt, and plans to ask the agriculture officer before deciding.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the choice after Neelam's question?
qa.a: Lalit admits he'd choose the gain, but the loss still feels bigger to him.

grounding: A young farmer imagines a loss and a gain of the same size and asks which she truly prefers, easing the pull toward the familiar crop.

He listed it for twenty thousand. The same model, used, was selling online for about nine.

passage:
Pranav, you're selling your phone for how much? Hmm. Sit. Your Sunaina aunty remembers something from when I was your age.

I shared a flat in Delhi with my friend Harish. He wanted to sell his old camera before going abroad. He asked for five thousand. Buyers kept offering two. He was furious. "Everyone's trying to cheat me."

I watched this for three weeks. Then I asked him, "Harish, if you walked into a shop and saw this camera, with that scratch on the lens, would you pay five thousand?"

He was silent. Then he said, "No. Maybe two."

"Then why should anyone else?"

He was annoyed with me for a day. But he sold it for two and a half the next week, before he left.

So, beta, would you pay what you're asking?

qa.q: How much did Harish ask for the camera?
qa.a: He asked for five thousand.

qa.q: What was young Sunaina feeling while watching Harish for three weeks?
qa.a: Young Sunaina felt frustrated and a bit worried, watching Harish refuse fair offers and feel cheated.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sunaina's story?
qa.a: Asking Harish whether he would pay five thousand for the camera in a shop made him see the buyer's view.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Sunaina asked the question?
qa.a: Harish felt annoyed with Sunaina for a day, but the question still helped him sell before he left.

grounding: An elder recalls a flatmate pricing a used camera far above offers, and asking if he would pay that price himself.

passage:
It was Navratri, and the whole family was going to the big garba ground. Dhruv refused to get into the car.

"I sit behind Papa. Always."

"Today Yogesh bhaiya is sitting there," said Mummy. "You sit by the window. You'll see the lights."

"No. Behind Papa."

At breakfast that morning, he had also refused the new poha and asked for plain toast, like every day. And he'd made them walk the long way to the temple, because it was the way he knew.

Yogesh bhaiya said, "Dhruv, the window seat is better tonight. The whole street has lights."

Dhruv sat stiffly by the window. For the first ten minutes, he stared straight ahead. Then a giant lit-up peacock passed, and he pressed his nose to the glass.

qa.q: Where did Dhruv always want to sit?
qa.a: Behind Papa.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv refuse the window seat, the new poha and the new route?
qa.a: Dhruv felt uneasy about change, because the usual seat, food and route felt safe and anything new felt risky.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv try the window seat?
qa.a: Yogesh bhaiya gave a reason to try it, the festival lights, and Dhruv was allowed to settle in slowly.

qa.q: How might Yogesh bhaiya feel when Dhruv pressed his nose to the glass?
qa.a: Yogesh bhaiya might feel pleased and amused that Dhruv enjoyed the window seat after all.

grounding: During a festival, a child insists on the same seat, breakfast and route, even when alternatives are fine.

"Manoj, it's Makar Sankranti. Try the til laddoo for breakfast."

"No, Jyoti didi. I want bread and jam."

"You have bread and jam every day."

"That's why I want it."

"And why won't you take the new bus route to school? It's shorter."

"The old route is the route."

"And your desk? Ma'am said you can move near the window."

"I like my desk."

"Manoj, why?"

He thought. "Because I know what happens. With new things, I don't know."

"But new things can be good too."

"Or bad."

Jyoti held out a small piece of laddoo. "Just one bite. If you hate it, bread and jam."

Manoj took the tiniest nibble. Chewed. "It's... okay."

"Only okay?"

"Maybe good. But tomorrow, bread and jam."

qa.q: What does Manoj have for breakfast every day?
qa.a: Bread and jam.

qa.q: Why does Manoj want to keep the same breakfast, route and desk?
qa.a: Manoj feels safer with the usual, because he knows what happens, and new things feel risky and uncertain.

qa.q: What did Jyoti didi do that helped Manoj try something new?
qa.a: Jyoti offered just one bite with a safe backup, so trying the laddoo felt small and low-risk.

qa.q: How does Jyoti didi seem to feel about Manoj's habits?
qa.a: Jyoti didi seems patient and gently amused, wanting Manoj to see that new things can be good too.

grounding: During a festival, a child sticks to the same breakfast, route and desk because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage:
I'm Jeevan. Last summer holidays, we went to Nani's house for a month.

On the first day, Urmila didi wanted to take a new path to the market, past the pond. I said no. We had to go the road way, the one we always took.

At lunch Nani made a new dish, jackfruit curry. I only ate rice and dal. I always eat rice and dal.

Urmila didi said, "Why don't you try one new thing?" I didn't want to. New things felt scary.

On the fifth day, she took me the pond way anyway. There were ducks and a little bridge! I loved it.

After that, I tried the jackfruit curry too. It was nice. But now I know new things aren't always bad.

qa.q: What new dish did Nani make at lunch?
qa.a: Jackfruit curry.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan refuse the new path and the new dish at first?
qa.a: Jeevan felt scared of new things, because the usual path and food felt safe and anything different felt risky.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan try new things?
qa.a: Urmila didi took Jeevan the pond way, and discovering the ducks and bridge made trying the curry easier too.

qa.q: How might Urmila didi have felt when Jeevan loved the pond path?
qa.a: Urmila didi probably felt happy and relieved that Jeevan finally enjoyed something new.

grounding: A child on summer holidays insists on the usual route and food because change feels risky, until a new path surprises them.

passage:
In Pablo's family in Valencia, everyone had done the science track at secondary school. His father was an engineer. His mother, a pharmacist. His sister Clara was studying medicine.

When the time came to choose his subjects for the last two years, Pablo just ticked science. He didn't think about it much. It was what everyone did.

But in the evenings he drew. Comic strips, portraits, the old tram outside the window. His art teacher had said, twice, that he should consider the arts track.

One night Clara found his sketchbook. "Pablo, these are amazing. Why are you doing science?"

He shrugged. "It's what we do."

"Did you choose it, or did you just not choose anything else?"

Pablo stared at her. He had never actually thought about it.

"Switching feels like a lot of trouble," he admitted. "And what if it's a mistake?"

"What if staying is?"

qa.q: What did Pablo draw in the evenings?
qa.a: Comic strips, portraits, the old tram outside the window.

qa.q: Why did Pablo tick science without much thought?
qa.a: Pablo felt that switching would be effortful and risky, so following the family's default felt easier and safer.

qa.q: What small step could Pablo take after Clara's question?
qa.a: Pablo could talk to his art teacher and parents about the arts track, and look at what switching would really involve.

qa.q: How might Clara feel about Pablo's choice?
qa.a: Clara seems concerned and encouraging, wanting Pablo to actually choose rather than drift.

grounding: A teenager abroad drifts into the family's default science track because switching feels risky, though he loves art.

passage:
In the school counsellor's room, Santosh sat with his stream-selection form. Commerce was already ticked.

"Why commerce?" asked Nilesh sir, the counsellor.

"My father did commerce. My uncle did commerce. My brother's doing commerce."

"And what do you enjoy?"

Santosh hesitated. "Biology. I like the labs."

"Then why not science?"

"It's a lot of work to switch now. The forms, the tuition, explaining it at home. And what if I'm wrong?"

Nilesh sir nodded. "That's a real worry. But I want to check something. Did you choose commerce, or did commerce just happen?"

Santosh looked at the form. He hadn't really chosen anything. He had just not changed anything.

"Can I take the form home for a week?" he asked.

"Of course. And bring your parents in if you want. I'll help you talk it through."

qa.q: Which subject does Santosh enjoy?
qa.a: Biology. I like the labs.

qa.q: Why had Santosh ticked commerce without choosing it?
qa.a: Santosh felt that switching would be a lot of work and risk, so going with the family's default felt safer.

qa.q: How did Nilesh sir help Santosh without pushing?
qa.a: Nilesh sir asked whether Santosh chose commerce or it just happened, took the worry seriously and offered to help talk with the parents.

qa.q: How might Santosh's father react if Santosh chooses science?
qa.a: His father might be surprised at first, but may feel proud if Santosh explains his love for biology.

grounding: A teenager drifts into the family's default commerce stream because switching feels effortful and risky.

passage:
Dear Rajni ma'am,

You asked me after class why I seemed unhappy with my subjects. I didn't answer properly, so I'm writing.

I'm in PCM. My parents didn't force me. Everyone in my family did PCM, so when the form came, I just ticked it. It felt like the normal thing.

But I hate physics. What I love is history and geography. I read about old maps for fun.

I've thought about switching to humanities. But then I think of all the forms, and telling my parents, and my friends asking why. It feels so much easier to just stay.

When you asked me, I realised I never actually decided PCM. It just happened because I didn't decide anything else.

Could we talk about what switching would really involve? I'm scared, but I think I'd rather choose than drift.

Thank you,
Sahil

qa.q: What does Sahil love to read about for fun?
qa.a: I read about old maps for fun.

qa.q: Why did Sahil stay in PCM despite hating physics?
qa.a: Sahil felt that switching would be a hassle and a risk, so staying felt easier, and the default became a choice never really made.

qa.q: What step is Sahil taking, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sahil is asking Rajni ma'am to talk through what switching involves, which turns drifting into an actual decision.

qa.q: How might Rajni ma'am feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rajni ma'am may feel touched and glad Sahil trusted her, and ready to help.

grounding: A teenager realises the family's default stream was never really chosen and writes to a teacher about choosing instead.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,

Guess what I finally did today? I switched my phone plan.

I know, very exciting. But listen. I had been on the same plan since Class 11. It cost more than double what the new ones cost, and gave half the data. Every month I'd see the bill and think, I should change. Then I'd think about calling customer care, the forms, the new SIM, and I'd just... not.

I told myself I was fine with it. "It works, why change?" But I wasn't fine. I just didn't want the effort.

This morning I timed it. The switch took twenty-two minutes.

Four years. Twenty-two minutes.

I'm now looking at everything else I've been "fine" with. My gym I never go to. The coaching I don't like. Maybe some of those are just inertia too.

Love,
Himani

qa.q: How long did the switch take?
qa.a: The switch took twenty-two minutes.

qa.q: Why did Himani stay on the old plan for so long?
qa.a: Himani felt the effort of switching was too much, and kept saying it was fine, so inertia felt like contentment.

qa.q: What could Himani do about the other things called "fine"?
qa.a: Himani could check each one, like the gym and coaching, and ask whether staying is a choice or just to avoid effort.

qa.q: How might Madhuri react to this letter?
qa.a: Madhuri might feel amused by the twenty-two minutes and encouraged to check Madhuri's own habits.

grounding: A young adult realises the overpriced phone plan lasted for years only because switching needed effort.

passage:
You want to know why I wasted a whole semester, Ujjwal? Okay. I'm Vidya, and it's a bit embarrassing.

In second year, I enrolled in a data analysis elective. By week three I knew it was badly taught. The lecturer read slides aloud. I learned more from free videos.

There was a much better elective, design thinking, with a great teacher. Switching was allowed until week five. All I had to do was fill one form and talk to the coordinator.

I kept meaning to. Every week, I'd think, next week. I told my friends, "It's fine, it's not that bad." And I honestly thought I was content.

Week five came and went. I stayed.

At the end of the semester, my friend who'd switched showed me her project. It was brilliant. I felt this sick drop in my stomach.

I wasn't content. I was just stuck. And I'd called it contentment so I wouldn't have to move.

qa.q: Until which week was switching allowed?
qa.a: Switching was allowed until week five.

qa.q: Why did Vidya stay in the weak elective?
qa.a: Vidya didn't want the small effort of switching and told herself it was fine, so inertia felt like contentment.

qa.q: What could Vidya do next time she notices a better option?
qa.a: Vidya could act on it straight away, like filling the form that day, instead of waiting for next week.

qa.q: How might Vidya's friend have felt showing her project?
qa.a: The friend probably felt proud and excited about the project, perhaps not realising how it made Vidya feel.

grounding: A young adult stays in a weak elective only because switching needs effort, and later sees the inertia was not contentment.

passage:
First week of July. Chinmay's PG was forty minutes from college by two buses. His friend Hrithik mentioned a new PG opening right next to campus, cheaper, with better food. "Come see it." Chinmay said, "Mine's fine."

Late August. Chinmay missed two morning lectures because of bus delays in the rain. He told Hrithik, "It's okay, I'm used to it." But he was tired every evening. The new PG still had a room free.

Early October. Hrithik sat on Chinmay's bed. "Why haven't you moved? It's closer, cheaper, better."

Chinmay opened his mouth to say "Mine's fine" again. Then he stopped. "Because moving is a whole thing. Packing, telling the owner, finding a van."

"So you're not happy here. You just don't want to move."

Chinmay looked around the cramped room. "I've been calling it fine because changing felt like work."

He went to see the new PG that evening.

qa.q: How far was Chinmay's PG from college?
qa.a: Forty minutes from college by two buses.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay keep saying his PG was fine?
qa.a: Chinmay felt that moving would be a hassle, so he told himself he was content even though he was tired and missing lectures.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say that helped Chinmay see the problem?
qa.a: Hrithik pointed out that Chinmay wasn't happy, just avoiding the effort of moving, which helped him see the inertia.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Chinmay finally went to see the new PG?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt relieved and pleased, having suggested it three months earlier.

grounding: Over three months, a young adult stays in a distant PG only because moving needs effort, calling it being fine.
